Composite materials are increasingly used in aircraft due to their high specific mechanical properties but are fragile to low velocity impacts.
Low velocity impacts can cause barely visible impact damage (BVID), characterized by small surface indentations and internal delaminations.
BVID can significantly degrade structural properties and lead to buckling failure under compressive loads.
Two nonlinear ultrasonic techniques, SIMONRAS and NWMS, were used to detect BVID in carbon fiber composite plates.
SIMONRAS measures resonance frequency shifts as excitation amplitude increases to detect nonlinear behavior caused by damage.
NWMS uses bi-tone excitation to detect harmonics and sidebands in the frequency spectrum indicative of nonlinear elastic response.
Test specimens were carbon fiber composite plates of 150 mm × 100 mm × 4 mm dimensions with unknown mechanical properties and damage size.
The first resonance frequency of the plates ranged between 160 and 200 Hz; the third resonance mode was around 2260 to 2320 Hz.
The nonlinear parameter 'a' was calculated from the resonance frequency shift and correlated with damage severity.
Larger delamination areas showed higher nonlinear parameter values and stronger harmonic and sideband amplitudes.
Harmonics observed included 2F1, 3F1, 4F1, and sidebands such as F2 ± F1 and F2 ± 2F1.
The experimental setup included a fixed-end composite plate excited by a speaker and measured by an accelerometer.
Nonlinear elastic wave spectroscopy (NEWS) methods are more sensitive than linear acoustic methods for detecting small cracks and delaminations.
Damage introduces nonlinearities such as hysteresis and discrete memory effects in the material's elastic response.
The nonlinear response is more sensitive to damage than changes in linear modulus.
The study confirms the potential of nonlinear ultrasonic methods for early detection of BVID in aircraft composites.
Further validation is required for different composite materials and lay-up configurations.
The nonlinear parameter 'a' increases with damage size even under the same excitation amplitude and boundary conditions.
Sideband amplitudes in NWMS tests depend on the damage severity and excitation amplitude.
The methods can detect damage even when it is not visually apparent on the composite surface.
